H.R. 4054 MAKES PROGRESS ON ACCREDITATION TRANSPARENCY
There are a few reforms in H.R. 4054 that are good steps towards improving clarity and transparency for accreditors and the accreditation process. Student Achievement Standards
Accreditors develop a robust set of standards that colleges must follow to remain fully accredited. Accreditors are required to develop standards around curricula, faculty, facilities, administrative and fiscal capability, student support services, admissions practices, program lengths and objectives, student complaints, and Title IV compliance.\35\ While most accreditors also measure student achievement outcomes by choice, there are no federal guidelines for student achievement outcomes or standardization across all accreditors and institutions. Congressional Republicans and Democrats, as well as student-focused advocates strongly believe Congress must formalize student achievement standards to better hold institutions accountable for their outcomes.\36\ Accrediting agencies argue that they would prefer to be self-regulated, but that has led to numerous variations in the scope of quality assurance.\37\
\35\20 U.S.C. Sec. 496(a)(5).
\36\Katherine Knott, Biden Administration Wants Accreditors to Set Benchmarks for Student Outcomes, Inside Higher Educ. (Mar. 15, 2024), https://www.insidehighered.com/news/government/2024/03/15/accreditors-may-have-set-student-achievement-benchmarks; Chazz Robinson, Emily Rounds, How Common Definitions for Student Achievement Can Strengthen College Accreditation, Third Way (Nov. 3, 2023), https:// www.thirdway.org/memo/how-common-definitions-for-student-achievement-can-strengthen-college-accreditation.
\37\Edward Conroy, If ``Outcomes Are Key'' in Higher Education, Why Do Accreditors Oppose Minimum Standards for Colleges?, New America (Mar. 5, 2024), https://www.newamerica.org/education-policy/edcentral/ why-do-accreditors-oppose-minimum-standards-for-colleges/.
H.R. 4054 proposes three new definitions of student achievement standards institutions must report to accreditors for the purpose of remaining in good standing: student success outcomes, learning outcomes, and labor market outcomes. While it is important for accreditors to assess these proposed student achievement outcome categories, Committee Democrats have concerns with how vague the standards are and whether they should address institutional variety. A more balanced approach would be to establish baseline requirements within the standards and then develop additional standards aligned for similar groups of institutions. Factoring in institutions' student demographics, institutional sector, and modality of instruction would allow for a more adequate comparison across similar programs, without compromising the foundational outcomes for which all institutions should be held accountable.
While this standardization is a good step, Committee Republicans ruined the possibility of thoughtful implementation because H.R. 4054 also prohibits accreditors from holding institutions accountable for any additional standards adopted, regardless of whether they may be helpful benchmarks to evaluate quality. Accrediting agencies have expressed significant concern with the elimination of this flexibility because it prevents them from ``driv[ing] institutional improvement . . . for institutions with different missions.''\38\
\38\Letter from Counc. of Reg. Accred. Commissions to Rep. Tim Walberg, Chair, House. Cmte. on Educ. & Workforce, 1 (June 24, 2025), https://www.neche.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/C-RAC-Letter-on-House- Accreditation-Choice-and-Innovation-Act-6.24.25.pdf.
Improved Transparency Within Accreditation Process
H.R. 4054 requires accrediting agencies to develop guidelines to eliminate conflicts of interest within accrediting boards or governing bodies. Further, it prohibits conflicts of interest on the NACIQI. One analysis showed that as of 2019, six of the fourteen prominent institutional accrediting agencies had at least two members serving in board positions with ``direct links to colleges, suggesting that they lack the necessary independence'' necessary to serve as independent reviewers.\39\ Lastly, H.R. 4054 directs the Secretary to develop common terminology for accrediting decisions, which will help streamline oversight and help institutions understand their responsibilities. These transparency policies will ensure that education executives who lobby for their industry or institution cannot also oversee the development of quality standards for accreditors or institutions. This recognition of conflict against the greater public interest will improve the creditability and integrity of the accreditation.\40\
\39\Ben Miller, Bolstering the Public Voice in Accreditation, Ctr. for Am. Prog. (Jun. 6, 2019), https://www.americanprogress.org/article/ bolstering-public-voice-accreditation/.
\40\Robert Shireman, Good and Bad in the Republican Higher Education Package, Accreditation Edition, The Century Found. (Jan. 29, 2024), https://tcf.org/content/commentary/good-and-bad-in-the-republican-higher-education-package-accreditation-edition/.
Regrettably, as discussed above, the rest of H.R. 4054 is significantly concerning and neither improves the ability of accreditors to make institutional quality determinations nor has any apparent effect on college costs.
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 4054
Committee Democrats did not put forward any amendments to improve the bill.
Conclusion
The ill-informed accreditation reforms put forth in H.R. 4054 will undoubtedly erode the quality and value of higher education. For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present unanimously opposed H.R. 4054 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on June 25, 2025. Unless there is drastic revision of H.R. 4054, we would urge the House of Representatives to oppose it as well.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
